passage: After choir practice Shalini caught Lalremsiami by the harmonium. "Your solo was amazing. Honestly the best thing I have ever heard in this school. You're a genius!" Lalremsiami said thanks and felt warm, and then Shalini added, "Can I copy your English notes tonight?" The warmth cooled a little. She thought about Mr Dutta, who had said the day before, "Your breath control on the long note has improved since August." That comment had named one thing and asked for nothing. "I can share the notes for one chapter," she said carefully. Shalini said, "Okay," cheerfully. Lalremsiami still didn't know for sure whether Shalini meant it. Perhaps she did, and had a request too.

qa.q: Where did Shalini catch Lalremsiami?
qa.a: She caught her by the harmonium after choir practice.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami's warm feeling cool after Shalini's request?
qa.a: She began to wonder if the big praise was leading up to the favour. She could not be sure, so she compared it with Mr Dutta's specific comment that asked for nothing.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami try next to understand Shalini's praise better?
qa.a: Notice whether Shalini's praise stays specific and continues when she asks for nothing, and keep her own answer about the notes calm and clear.

qa.q: How might Shalini see her own praise?
qa.a: She may honestly admire the solo and simply feel comfortable asking for notes.

grounding: Praise can be genuine, strategic or teasing, and the teen checks specificity and whether a request follows.

passage:
Dear Gopika didi,

You asked how the new class is going. Mostly fine, but I have a puzzle. A girl in my row, Esha, keeps saying things like, "You're the smartest person in the school, Sangeeta." I like hearing it, but I noticed she says it right before asking to borrow my pen, my notes or my seat. Meanwhile, my art teacher told me last week that my shading on the apple had gotten softer, and she asked me for nothing.

I don't want to be unfair to Esha, because I don't actually know her reasons. So I'm just watching whether her kind words show up when she doesn't need something. What do you think? 🤔

Love, Sangeeta

qa.q: Who says Sangeeta is the smartest person in the school?
qa.a: A girl in Sangeeta's row, Esha, says it.

qa.q: Why does Sangeeta hesitate to trust Esha's praise?
qa.a: Sangeeta noticed the compliments come just before Esha asks to borrow something, so Sangeeta wonders if the praise is a way to get a favour. Sangeeta admits not knowing Esha's reasons.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do that is both fair and careful?
qa.a: Keep watching whether Esha's kindness appears when she needs nothing, and decide about lending her things calmly one at a time.

qa.q: How might Esha feel if she knew Sangeeta was watching her praise?
qa.a: She may feel misjudged if she meant it, or caught out if she did not.

grounding: A teenager compares specific, request-free praise with flattery and admits motives cannot be confirmed.

passage:
Urmila, you asked why I stopped going to the art room at lunch. Okay. I'm Payal, and I'm going to tell you the full thing.
So Vikrant from Class 12 started saying, every day, "Payal, you're the most talented artist in the school." Every day. Same sentence. I felt amazing at first, honestly.
But it was always the same line, never about a drawing. He never said which one. And then, week three, he said, "Since you're so talented, can you do the charts for my project?"
I'm not saying he was lying. Maybe he meant it and also needed help. I can't know what he was thinking. But I noticed three things: nothing specific, same words daily, then a request.
Compare that with Mrs Bhat, who said my shading on the jug was careful. Once. And never asked for anything.

qa.q: What did Vikrant ask Payal to do in week three?
qa.a: He asked her to do the charts for his project.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling about Vikrant's praise by the end?
qa.a: Payal had gone from feeling amazing to wary and unsure, because the praise was never specific and ended in a request.

qa.q: What could Payal do next time praise sounds like this?
qa.a: Payal could look for the same cues, whether praise is specific, consistent and free of a request, while remembering they are hints, not proof.

qa.q: How might Mrs Bhat's praise have felt different to Payal?
qa.a: It probably felt genuine and trustworthy, because it named a real detail, the shading on the jug, and came without asking for anything.

grounding: The monologue shows a teenager checking praise for specificity, consistency and a hidden request, without claiming to know the motive.

passage:
I'm Madhav, and I was there when the new boy, Rishab, sat down next to Naveen at break.
"Bro, your bowling is legendary," Rishab said. "Legend. Seriously."
Naveen grinned. He's our best fast bowler and he knows it.
Rishab kept going for five minutes. Then: "Can I borrow your cycle after school? Just today."
I watched Naveen's grin fade a little. He didn't answer straight away. He asked, "Which match did you see me bowl in?"
Rishab hesitated. "The... the big one."
I have no idea what Rishab was really thinking. Maybe he'd heard about Naveen from someone. Maybe he was just nervous being new.
Naveen said, "Let me think about the cycle. But come to nets tomorrow, you can watch properly." Rishab came. Later he said Naveen's yorker was unreal, and this time he named the match.

qa.q: What did Rishab ask to borrow?
qa.a: He asked to borrow Naveen's cycle after school.

qa.q: What might Naveen have been thinking when his grin faded?
qa.a: Naveen probably felt doubtful and a bit wary, wondering if the praise was a set-up for the cycle request rather than genuine admiration.

qa.q: Which choice of Naveen's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking which match Rishab had seen was a kind way to check if the praise was specific, and inviting him to nets gave the praise a chance to become real.

qa.q: How might Rishab have seen the conversation?
qa.a: Being new, Rishab may have felt nervous and used big praise to make friends quickly, so he was probably relieved to be invited to nets.

grounding: A friend's account shows a teenager checking whether praise is specific and free of a request, without assuming the motive.

passage:
Week 1: After choir, Chetan told Chandrika, "The high note in the second verse, you held it without wobbling." She thanked him and wondered if he wanted something. He didn't ask for anything.
Week 2: He mentioned how she came in exactly on the beat after the long rest, which nobody else in the altos managed. Again, nothing asked. Chandrika's friend said, "Maybe he likes you. Or maybe he's buttering you up for the solo."
Chandrika thought about it on the walk home. His praise was specific. It was the same kind every week. And he never asked for anything.
Week 3: Chetan got the solo. Chandrika braced herself for him to go quiet. Instead, after rehearsal, he said, "Your bridge section today was better than mine."
She still couldn't know exactly what he felt. But she decided to take it as real.

qa.q: What did Chetan say about the high note in Week 1?
qa.a: He said she held the high note in the second verse without wobbling.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when her friend suggested Chetan might be buttering her up?
qa.a: She felt uncertain and a little suspicious, wondering if the praise was strategic, until she thought through the cues on the walk home.

qa.q: How did Chandrika use the cues well?
qa.a: She checked whether the praise was specific, consistent and free of a request over three weeks, and still admitted she couldn't know his feelings for sure.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan had asked for a favour in Week 2?
qa.a: Chandrika would have had more reason to wonder whether the praise was flattery tied to what he wanted.

grounding: The before, during and after beats show a teenager reading praise over time for specificity, consistency and absence of a request, without claiming certainty.

passage: You're asking whether that senior's compliments are real, Swati? Then let your Thomas Uncle tell you about 1989. I was in class ten at a boys' school in Bangalore, and a senior, Victor, started calling me "the best spinner in the city". Every day. Loudly. I floated for a week. Then one evening he said, "Such a genius bowler can surely write my history project, no?" And I did it, twice, before it clicked. Meanwhile our games teacher, Mr Pinto, hardly ever praised me. But when he did, it was small and exact: "Your wrist was straighter today, keep that." He said the same thing whether others were listening or not, and he never asked me for anything. I'm not saying Victor was a crook. Maybe he half meant it; I'll never know. But I learned to listen for the specific, the steady, and the favour that follows. Now pass me that tea before it goes cold.

qa.q: What did Victor call Thomas every day?
qa.a: Victor called Thomas "the best spinner in the city".

qa.q: What was young Thomas feeling during that first week of praise?
qa.a: Thomas was flattered and happy, floating for a week; after writing the project twice he likely felt foolish and used, though Victor may have half meant it.

qa.q: Which choice in the story would you have made differently, and why?
qa.a: Young Thomas could have paused when the favour arrived right after the compliments; noticing that the praise came with a request would have saved him writing the project twice.

qa.q: How might Mr Pinto have seen his own small, exact comments?
qa.a: Mr Pinto likely saw them as honest coaching, saying the same thing whether others were listening or not, with nothing wanted in return.

grounding: It shows an elder's memory of strategic praise versus specific, consistent praise with no request attached, while admitting motives can't be confirmed from words alone.
